name: The I-75 Spine
description:
Interstate 75 was built to move cars. In 2200, it moves everything else. The I-75 Spine runs 450 kilometers from Detroit's northern border to the Mackinac Bridge, forming the primary ground transportation corridor through Michigan's lower peninsula. The highway has been widened to twelve lanes — six automated cargo, four high-speed passenger, two emergency/military — and the entire corridor is sovereign infrastructure operated by Ferrogate Transit under a Michigan state charter. Ferrogate controls the traffic, maintains the surface, and charges the tolls, which makes the Spine the most profitable 450 kilometers of road in the Great Lakes Metropolitan Area.

The corridor is not just a highway. It is a linear economy. Service stations every 30 kilometers have evolved into waystation complexes — refueling, cargo transfer, passenger staging, and the commercial services that develop wherever traffic concentrates. The waystations are Ferrogate sovereign territory, which means the law on the highway is Ferrogate's law, and the law between waystations is whatever the speed of your vehicle allows you to outrun. The Spine's automated cargo lanes run 24 hours without human intervention, hauling materials between Detroit's manufacturing zones and the UP's extraction facilities via the Mackinac Bridge. The passenger lanes are slower, more surveilled, and more expensive — Ferrogate's pricing algorithm charges by time of day, tier rating, and destination, ensuring that the road's capacity serves those who can pay.

The communities along the Spine — Flint, Saginaw's southern suburbs, Grayling, Gaylord — have been absorbed into the corridor's economy like organs along an intestinal tract. They exist to service the traffic. Their populations work in the waystations, maintain the road infrastructure, and provide the human labor that the automated systems haven't replaced yet. The Spine is Michigan's central nervous system: sever it, and the lower peninsula loses contact with the UP, Detroit loses access to extraction resources, and the cargo flow that sustains the eastern GLM's manufacturing base stops. Everyone knows this. The Spine is defended accordingly.

sights: Twelve lanes of traffic — six automated cargo lanes moving in synchronized convoys, four passenger lanes, two military
Waystation complexes every 30 kilometers, glowing with service lights and Ferrogate branding
Automated cargo convoys — massive vehicles moving in tight formation at speeds that would kill a human driver
Michigan forest pressing in on both sides of the corridor — the landscape the highway cut through and never fully displaced
Military checkpoint infrastructure at key interchanges — the Spine is critical infrastructure and looks it
sounds: The constant rush of high-speed traffic — a wall of sound that the corridor communities live inside
Automated cargo vehicles communicating in machine frequencies — a conversation you hear as static
Waystation commerce — the sounds of refueling, maintenance, and transaction
The Spine at 3 AM — quieter but never silent, the automated lanes maintaining their rhythm through the dark
smells: Electric motor ozone from the automated convoys
Waystation food service — the smell of franchise nutrition, standardized across 450 kilometers
Michigan pine on cross-winds, briefly overriding the corridor's industrial baseline
atmosphere.feel: Linear. The Spine has one dimension — north-south — and everything about it is oriented along that axis. You are either moving toward Detroit or moving toward the Bridge, and the corridor is designed to make that movement fast, profitable, and controlled. Stopping is an economic activity. Turning off is a navigational challenge. The Spine wants to move you, and the Spine gets what it wants.

demographics: Corridor population approximately 800,000, distributed across waystation communities and surviving towns. The population is transit-dependent — their livelihoods exist because the traffic exists. Tier 2 majority, with Ferrogate employees at Tier 3. The communities are young, transient, and oriented toward the road rather than toward each other.
economy: Transit tolls (Ferrogate Transit), waystation commerce, and corridor maintenance. The Spine generates revenue proportional to the cargo and passenger volume it carries, which is substantial — 60% of Michigan's north-south commerce moves on this road. The waystation economy provides services to that traffic. The corridor communities provide labor to the waystations.
power_structure: Ferrogate Transit sovereign authority over the highway and waystations. Michigan state authority over the spaces between. Military infrastructure at key interchanges under federal authority. The three jurisdictions coexist because the Spine must function, and dysfunction would cost more than cooperation.
dangers: Automated convoy accidents — rare but catastrophic, involving tonnage that reshapes the landscape
Waystation sovereignty gaps — Ferrogate law applies on the highway, state law applies off it, and the transition is exploitable
The Spine as military target — in any escalation of the UP war, the highway becomes the first strategic objective
Toll pricing as economic control — Ferrogate's algorithm determines who can afford to travel, which determines who can access the UP
Corridor communities' total dependence on traffic — any disruption to the Spine is an immediate livelihood crisis
opportunities: Cargo interception — the automated convoys are efficient but not invulnerable, and the cargo they carry is valuable
Waystation contracts — Ferrogate outsources maintenance and service operations, and the contracts are available to those who qualify
Intelligence on cargo movement — the Spine's traffic data reveals the GLM's economic activity in real time
Alternative route knowledge — the old surface roads still exist, and knowing them when the Spine closes is worth something
story_hooks: Ferrogate's automated convoy system has been rerouting specific cargo to unauthorized destinations — the highway is stealing its own freight
A waystation community has blockaded the Spine, demanding equitable toll revenue sharing — the first infrastructure strike in the GLM
Military assets are massing at the Spine's northern terminus near the Mackinac Bridge, and Ferrogate has been ordered to clear civilian traffic — an operation is coming

adjacent_to: Bluewater Checkpoint (Port Huron, via I-69 interchange)

frequented_by: Automated cargo convoys and the technicians who monitor them
Passenger traffic between Detroit and the UP
Ferrogate Transit employees operating the waystations
Military convoys heading north to the UP contested zone

notable_locations.name: Waystation 7 (Flint)
notable_locations.description: The largest waystation complex on the Spine — a small city built around a highway interchange, processing more daily traffic than most ports

notable_locations.name: The Grayling Military Interchange
notable_locations.description: Federal military staging facility at the corridor's midpoint — where civilian infrastructure meets military logistics

notable_locations.name: Bridge Approach Zone
notable_locations.description: The final 20 kilometers before the Mackinac Bridge — the point where the Spine narrows, traffic converges, and control is absolute
